prompt: What does an organisational unit hold?
hint: It is a folder in the tree.

choices.text: Resources shared by the accounts beneath it
choices.why: An OU holds no resources at all. Each resource still belongs to exactly one account.

choices.text: Accounts and other OUs, never a resource
choices.why: Right. It is a branch of the tree, so that a rule can be attached once for everything in it.

choices.text: The IAM users of a department
choices.why: Users live inside accounts. An OU groups accounts, and is drawn by the kind of work, not the team.

choices.text: A bill of its own, paid by its first account
choices.why: There is one bill for the whole organisation, paid by the management account.

prompt: Right after `create-account`, where in the tree is the new account?
hint: The command takes no parent.

choices.text: In the OU named after it, which is created with it
choices.why: No OU is created for an account. OUs are made with `create-organizational-unit`, on purpose.

choices.text: Nowhere, until `move-account` gives it a parent
choices.why: Every account always has exactly one parent; the tree has no loose accounts.

choices.text: Directly under the root, beside the management account
choices.why: Right. The transcript's `list-children` of the root listed all six until the moves.

choices.text: In the same OU as the account that created it
choices.why: The management account sits under the root, and so does every account it creates, but not because it is there.

prompt: `shop-prod` already exists under the root of a new organisation with no OUs. Order the steps that put it into `Prod`, under `Workloads`.
hint: Each step needs an id that the step before it produced.
items: look up the root's id with `list-roots`
create the OU `Workloads` under the root
trap: Creating `Prod` before `Workloads` is the usual slip: `create-organizational-unit` needs the parent's id, and `Workloads` has none until it exists.

prompt: A company draws its tree by department: an OU for marketing, one for engineering, one for finance, each holding production and test accounts. What will its rules struggle with?
hint: A rule attached to an OU reaches every account below it.

choices.text: Nothing; a department is the natural owner of a rule
choices.why: Rules follow the kind of work. A department mixes production with tests, so its branch cannot carry either kind's rules.

choices.text: Its bill, which can only be split by OU
choices.why: The bill lists every account, whatever OU it sits in. The tree's shape does not decide the invoice.

choices.text: Nesting, since three departments exceed five levels
choices.why: Three OUs side by side are one level. Depth is not the problem here.

choices.text: Rules for live systems end up repeated in three places
choices.why: Right. Production is spread across three branches, so no single branch can hold the rule. That is why the shop groups by `Prod` and `Staging`.

prompt: moto's root lists no enabled policy type right after `create-organization` with all features. What would AWS's root list?
hint: The API reference for `CreateOrganization` says it.

choices.text: Service control policies, enabled at once
choices.why: Right. AWS enables them in the root when the organisation is created with all features; moto waits for `enable-policy-type`.

choices.text: Nothing either, until the first account joins
choices.why: Joining accounts does not enable a policy type. The empty list is moto's difference.

choices.text: Every policy type AWS offers
choices.why: Only service control policies are on from the start. The others are enabled one by one.

choices.text: Consolidated billing, which is a policy type
choices.why: Consolidated billing is a feature set, not a policy type, and it is always there.

prompt: The top of an organisation's tree, with an id starting `r-`, is called the ___.
hint: One per organisation.

prompt: Two accounts each send 8,192 GB from `sa-east-1` to the internet in a month: 0.15 per GB for the first 10,240 GB, then 0.138. In one organisation, how many dollars is the month, leaving the free allowance aside?
hint: Price 16,384 GB as one account would.

prompt: Same two accounts, but `shop-staging` sends only 2,048 GB while `shop-prod` sends 8,192 GB. How many dollars does the organisation save against two separate bills?
hint: Add them first, then see whether the total crosses 10,240 GB.

prompt: What changes when an account that paid its own bill joins an organisation?
hint: Who pays, and how usage is counted.

choices.text: Its resources move into the management account
choices.why: Nothing moves. Ownership stays with the member; only the payer changes.

choices.text: Somebody else pays, and its use is priced with the rest
choices.why: Right. One payer, and AWS prices the organisation as if it were one account where prices have tiers.

choices.text: Its charges disappear from the invoice, merged into one total
choices.why: Each member is still listed with what it used. The invoice is one, the lines are per account.

choices.text: Its prices drop to the management account's region
choices.why: Prices follow the region a resource runs in, whoever pays. Joining changes no price list.

prompt: Which of these are shared across an organisation's accounts by default? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three things cross the walls on the bill.

choices.text: The volume tiers of a price
choices.why: Right. Usage is added up across the accounts before the tiers are applied.

choices.text: A Savings Plan's discount
choices.why: Right. By default it applies to matching use in any account; lesson 14 reads it.

choices.text: The VPC quota of each region
choices.why: Quotas stay per account, which is one of the reasons to split accounts at all.

choices.text: Credits granted by AWS
choices.why: Right. They are spent against the whole organisation unless the billing preferences restrict them.

choices.text: The IAM users of the management account
choices.why: Identities never cross the walls. Billing is the part that does.

prompt: A company created its organisation with `CONSOLIDATED_BILLING` years ago and now wants guardrails. What stands in the way?
hint: Read what the API reference for `EnableAllFeatures` asks for.

choices.text: Nothing: policies can be attached in a billing-only organisation
choices.why: A billing-only organisation can attach no policy of any kind. It needs all features first.

choices.text: The organisation has to be deleted and made again
choices.why: The move to all features exists for exactly this case. Nothing is deleted.

choices.text: Every invited account has to approve the change first
choices.why: Right. Enabling all features sends a handshake to each invited account, and the change waits for all of them.

choices.text: Every member account has to be created again
choices.why: The accounts stay as they are; what they owe the change is an approval.

prompt: Where do this section's numbers about money come from, given that moto has no bill?
hint: One program from lesson 1, and some arithmetic.

choices.text: From `aws ce get-cost-and-usage` against moto
choices.why: moto answered it with an empty list. It keeps no usage and computes no charge.

choices.text: From AWS's published price list, and arithmetic on it
choices.why: Right. The tiers were printed by `price.py` from the offer of 16 September 2026, and the bill was worked out by hand.

choices.text: From a real organisation's invoice
choices.why: There is no AWS account behind the course, so there is no invoice to read.

choices.text: From moto's own price table
choices.why: moto has no price table. A price from moto would be a price nobody published.

prompt: Why should the shop's first web server not run in the management account?
hint: What applies to every member and not to it?

choices.text: Machines there are billed at a higher price
choices.why: A machine costs the same in any account. The reason is what governs it.

choices.text: It has no default VPC to put the server in
choices.why: Every account has a default VPC in every region, the management account's included.

choices.text: Guardrails never apply to it, and it reaches every member
choices.why: Right. A workload there runs outside every rule, in the one account whose compromise is everybody's.

choices.text: Its quotas are a fraction of a member's
choices.why: It has the same default quotas as any other account.

prompt: In moto, `list-attached-role-policies` for `shop-prod`'s `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` answered an empty list. What would it answer in AWS, for an account the organisation created?
hint: AWS gives the role what it needs to administer the account.

choices.text: An empty list as well, until somebody attaches a policy
choices.why: That is moto's behaviour. AWS attaches a policy when it creates the role.

choices.text: `ReadOnlyAccess`, so that the management account can only look
choices.why: The role exists to administer the account, not to look at it.

choices.text: `AdministratorAccess`
choices.why: Right. Taking the role on gives full control of the member account, which is why the management account is guarded so closely.

choices.text: The organisation's service control policies
choices.why: An SCP is attached in Organizations, never to a role. Lesson 4 says what it does.

prompt: The trust policy of `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` names `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root`. Who may take the role on?
hint: `root` at the end of an account's ARN is not the root user.

choices.text: Only the management account's root user
choices.why: The word reads that way and means the account as a whole. Lesson 9 reads trust policies properly.

choices.text: Whoever in that account its IAM lets through
choices.why: Right. The trust policy lets the account in; the account's IAM decides which of its identities may use that.

choices.text: Any account of the organisation
choices.why: Only the account it names. `shop-staging` is not `123456789012`.

choices.text: The root of the organisation's tree, `r-ucqy`
choices.why: The tree's root is not an identity and cannot take a role on. The ARN names an account.

prompt: Put the joining of an existing account in order.
hint: The account itself has the last word.
items: AWS e-mails the other account's owner
an administrator there creates `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` by hand
trap: Expecting the role to exist after joining is the usual slip: only accounts the organisation creates get it.

prompt: `invite-account-to-organization` answered `500` in moto. What does that mean?
hint: Whose error is a 500 here?

choices.text: AWS refused the invitation because `111122223333` does not exist
choices.why: Nothing reached AWS; the request went to moto, and moto failed.

choices.text: moto does not implement invitations
choices.why: Right. The handshake was described from AWS's documentation and not run.

choices.text: The invited account must be created first with `create-account`
choices.why: An invitation is for an account that already exists outside the organisation.

choices.text: The organisation has reached its limit of accounts
choices.why: A limit would be a refusal with a reason. A 500 is the server failing.

prompt: `shop-staging`, created inside the organisation, tries `leave-organization` the next day. What stops it, with no guardrail in place?
hint: It would become a standalone account.

choices.text: Nothing; a member may leave whenever it likes
choices.why: A member may leave, but not before it has what a standalone account needs.

choices.text: Only the management account may remove an account
choices.why: `leave-organization` is run from inside the member, and it exists for exactly that.

choices.text: It lacks a payment method and a support plan
choices.why: Right. A created account never collected them, and a standalone account needs all three.

choices.text: Accounts created by an organisation can never leave it
choices.why: They can, once the missing details are added. Lesson 4's guardrail is what forbids it outright.

prompt: Match each command to what it answered in this lesson.
hint: One transcript each.

pairs.left: `list-children` of the root, after the moves

prompt: An existing account with five years of history joins the shop's organisation by invitation. Which of these is true of it afterwards?
hint: Compare a created account with an invited one.

choices.text: Its resources become the management account's
choices.why: Joining moves no resource. It keeps every wall.

choices.text: It already carries `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`
choices.why: Only created accounts get the role. An invited one gets it when somebody creates it there.

choices.text: It stays under the root forever, since only created accounts can be moved
choices.why: Any member can be moved between OUs, whichever way it joined.

choices.text: Its usage now counts towards the organisation's volume tiers
choices.why: Right. From joining on, the management account pays for it and prices it with everybody else's usage.

prompt: A teammate proposes giving `security` its own organisation, so that nobody in the shop's organisation can touch it. What does the shop lose?
hint: What do two organisations not share?

choices.text: One bill, and the rules attached to its tree
choices.why: Right. Two organisations are two payers and two trees. An account is better protected in its own OU with guardrails than outside the tree.

choices.text: Nothing, since two organisations may share an OU between them
choices.why: An OU belongs to one tree, and an account to one organisation at a time.

choices.text: The account's default VPC
choices.why: The default VPC belongs to the account, whatever organisation it is in.

choices.text: The ability to create IAM users in it
choices.why: IAM lives inside the account and works the same in any organisation, or none.
